Where Do LLM Ensemble Gains Come From?
Decomposing Candidate Value, Diversity, and Aggregation

Donghwan Kim Affiliation: Independent Researcher
Abstract

LLM ensemble gains are often measured against a single baseline, but the value attributed to additional candidates can change with the comparison used. We study an LLM aggregator under four matched conditions: Direct (no candidates), Single-slot (one candidate in a multi-slot interface), Duplicate (one candidate repeated), and Multi-candidate (separately generated candidates). Under either non-diverse control, overall candidate gain (CIV) splits algebraically into an additional-candidate contrast (DSV) and a candidate-context contrast (CCV); the split, but not CIV, depends on the chosen control. On MultiHopRAG model diversity (k=2k{=}2), the repetition gap Rep=−8.33\mathrm{Rep}=-8.33 pp [−13.25,−3.75][-13.25,-3.75] quantifies the difference between gains measured against Duplicate and Single-slot. On a matched FRAMES stronger-panel extension (n=200n{=}200, k=3k{=}3, aggregator output limit 4096), paired Δ​Rep=+9.67\Delta\mathrm{Rep}=+9.67 pp [+6.00,+13.50][+6.00,+13.50]; within panels, Rep changes sign (original −6.33-6.33; stronger +3.33+3.33). In FRAMES evidence aggregation, candidate-context contrasts remain strongly negative under both non-diverse controls. Our results show why ensemble evaluations should state the reference control before attributing gains to additional candidates.

1 Introduction

Work on LLM ensembles usually asks whether more samples, models, or evidence raise final accuracy (Wang et al., 2023; Du et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024). Beyond majority voting, Universal Self-Consistency uses an LLM to select among free-form candidate answers (Chen et al., 2023), while LLM-Blender ranks and fuses outputs from different models (Jiang et al., 2023). These methods show that combining candidates involves a decision about how their information is used. Adding models is not always beneficial (Li et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026). Multi-agent debate also does not consistently outperform simpler self-consistency or ensembling methods (Smit et al., 2024). This makes it important to distinguish the value of additional candidates from the behavior of the system that combines them. A separate audit finds that common diversity metrics often re-express capability, and that latent complementarity rarely becomes majority-vote gain (Kim, 2026a). In tool-mediated industrial diagnosis, specialist information likewise need not turn into a matching gain for an LLM integrator (Kim, 2026c).

Overall accuracy alone does not reveal why an ensemble succeeds or fails. This is a longstanding issue in ensemble learning. Classical work relates ensemble error to diversity among predictors (Krogh and Vedelsby, 1994; Brown et al., 2005). More recently, Choi et al. (2025) separate the effects of voting and debate, while Ali (2026) decomposes majority-vote gains into rescued and damaged predictions. These studies show why aggregate performance can hide important differences between ensemble mechanisms. We do not claim to be the first decomposition of ensemble gains. Our contribution is a matched set of answer-level controls for an LLM aggregator that can generate a new answer rather than only selecting a member prediction. We test whether Duplicate and Single-slot, two plausible non-diverse controls, yield the same attribution of candidate value; they do not, and their accuracy gap changes sign between the evaluated candidate-generation configurations.

We organize the measurement around four questions:

  1. 1.

    Does a Multi-candidate panel help relative to Direct solving (no candidate answers)?

  2. 2.

    How does Multi-candidate compare with Single-slot, which places one candidate in the same multi-slot interface?

  3. 3.

    How does that comparison change when the baseline is Duplicate, which repeats one candidate across slots?

  4. 4.

    What does the gap between Duplicate and Single-slot reveal about the attributed value of additional candidates?

The central empirical finding is that the value attributed to additional candidates depends on the non-diverse control.

Two settings make the dependence concrete. On MultiHopRAG model diversity (k=2k{=}2), gain over Duplicate is large (DSVdup=+9.3\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=+9.3 pp [+5.0,+14.0][+5.0,+14.0]) while overall candidate gain over Direct is −3.0-3.0 pp (CI includes zero). Under Single-slot, the same panel yields only DSVslot=+1.00\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}=+1.00 pp [−2.33,+4.67][-2.33,+4.67], matching a negative repetition gap (Rep=−8.33\mathrm{Rep}=-8.33 pp [−13.25,−3.75][-13.25,-3.75]). On FRAMES, a matched stronger-candidate extension (n=200n{=}200) raises total candidate gain by about +20.5+20.5 pp while changing the estimated gain of additional candidates by +10.3+10.3 pp under Single-slot but only +0.7+0.7 pp under Duplicate; within panels, Rep changes sign (original −6.33-6.33; stronger +3.33+3.33), with paired Δ​Rep=+9.67\Delta\mathrm{Rep}=+9.67 pp [+6.00,+13.50][+6.00,+13.50]. Separately, evidence-mediated candidate context remains strongly negative under both controls at a 4096-token aggregator ceiling.

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    Controlled decomposition. Matched Direct / Single-slot / Duplicate / Multi-candidate conditions (experiment IDs C2 / C1slot / C3b / C1) separate overall candidate gain (CIV), baseline-specific diversity contrasts (DSVdup\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}, DSVslot\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}), candidate-context contrasts (CCV), and the repetition gap (Rep\mathrm{Rep}), with elementary identities CIV=DSV+CCV\mathrm{CIV}=\mathrm{DSV}+\mathrm{CCV} and DSVdup=DSVslot−Rep\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}-\mathrm{Rep}. The accounting is algebraic; the contribution is the empirical controls and their interpretation.

  2. 2.

    Control dependence with a matched stress test. On MultiHop model diversity and on a matched FRAMES stronger-panel extension (n=200n{=}200, 4096-token aggregation), the estimated value of additional candidates changes with the non-diverse control. We do not claim Single-slot is uniquely neutral or isolates a pure causal diversity effect.

  3. 3.

    Effects beyond baseline choice. Evidence CCVslot\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{slot}} and CCVdup\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{dup}} remain strongly negative under both controls; raw-evidence restoration and aggregator-configuration comparisons identify losses that are not explained by choosing Duplicate versus Single-slot.

2 Related Work

Self-consistency, Universal Self-Consistency, multi-agent debate, generative fusion, sampling-and-voting, and mixture-of-agents all combine multiple generations (Wang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Du et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Self-MoA and related work ask whether mixing models helps when proposer quality varies (Li et al., 2025; Abdulaal et al., 2025). Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat simpler ensembling unless carefully tuned (Smit et al., 2024), and voting can account for much of the gain attributed to debate (Choi et al., 2025; Kaesberg et al., 2025).

Classical ensemble theory relates accuracy to disagreement among predictors (Krogh and Vedelsby, 1994; Brown et al., 2005; Kuncheva and Whitaker, 2003); recent LLM work likewise finds that diversity measures need not predict ensemble accuracy (Kim, 2026a; Ali, 2026; Chen, 2026). Kim (2026a) examines diversity metrics as predictors of majority-vote gain, whereas we study how non-diverse aggregation controls affect the attribution of candidate value. We do not claim the same bias-variance-covariance algebra for LLM answer accuracy; we use those results only as motivation for separating mechanism-level contrasts from a single aggregate gain.

Selector quality can matter more than diversity in generate-then-select pipelines (Maryanskyy et al., 2026). Other work studies trace-level synthesis in mixture-of-agents settings (Fadnavis et al., 2026). LLM-as-a-judge is widely used (Zheng et al., 2023), but producing candidates and selecting among them remain distinct capabilities. Prior work has also documented limitations of judge scores as optimization signals in a separate table-recognition setting (Kim, 2026b). Designed evidence asymmetry can help when deliberation is built for it (Li et al., 2026); long-context work shows that available information need not be used (Liu et al., 2024). In RAG-style aggregation of multiple evidence documents, models can favor repeated paraphrases and presentation order over independent support (Naphade, 2026). That line of work studies how models weight repeated evidence. We instead measure how candidate-level value attribution changes under matched Duplicate and Single-slot answer controls. We add a matched Direct / Single-slot / Duplicate / Multi-candidate contrast that separates candidate-mediated context from baseline-specific diversity increments.

3 Decomposing Ensemble Value

3.1 Four aggregation conditions

Fix one question, a panel of size kk, and an aggregator AA. Figure 1 shows four matched input constructions (reader-facing names first; experiment IDs in parentheses):

  • •

    Direct (C2): AA solves the question with no candidate answers. In sampling/model settings the prompt is closed-book; in evidence settings the frozen primary Direct condition is a matched evidence-conditioned direct solve.

  • •

    Single-slot (C1slot): the same kk-slot candidate interface with one filled candidate and k−1k{-}1 empty slots. For k=3k{=}3, the primary construction is [ci,empty,empty][c_{i},\text{empty},\text{empty}] with the first slot filled and placeholder “(No answer was provided for this slot.)”. Reported accuracy averages over candidate index ii, not over slot position (position and placeholder wording are later sensitivities).

  • •

    Duplicate (C3b): kk constructed copies of one candidate, [ci,ci,ci][c_{i},c_{i},c_{i}] for k=3k{=}3, averaged over candidate index ii.

  • •

    Multi-candidate (C1): kk separately generated candidate blocks. Final answer strings may still coincide.

Aggregator prompts for Single-slot, Duplicate, and Multi-candidate are candidate-only: raw evidence is not reinjected into those arms. Sampling, evidence, and the matched stronger-candidate extension use k=3k{=}3. The MultiHop and FRAMES model-diversity results we highlight use a pairwise (k=2k{=}2) unit.

3.2 Overall candidate gain

CIV (candidate-information value) is Multi-candidate minus Direct:

CIV=Acc⁡(C1)−Acc⁡(C2).\mathrm{CIV}=\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C1})-\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C2}). (1)

It is the accuracy difference relative to the matched Direct condition. The difference can be positive, near zero, or negative; negative CIV means the Multi-candidate setup underperforms Direct on that unit.

3.3 Gains over alternative non-diverse controls

DSVslot is Multi-candidate minus Single-slot:

DSVslot=Acc⁡(C1)−Acc⁡(C1slot).\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}=\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C1})-\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C1}_{\mathrm{slot}}). (2)

It asks how much accuracy changes when separately generated candidates replace one filled slot in the same interface. Adding candidates also changes how much candidate text is present, so this is not a pure causal diversity estimand.

DSVdup is Multi-candidate minus Duplicate:

DSVdup=Acc⁡(C1)−Acc⁡(C3b).\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C1})-\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C3b}). (3)

It asks how much accuracy changes when separately generated candidates replace constructed repetitions of one answer. The two baselines answer different questions; both are useful, and neither is uniquely “the” diversity effect. In historical primary tables, bare “DSV” means DSVdup\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}.

3.4 The repetition gap

Rep is Duplicate minus Single-slot:

Rep=Acc⁡(C3b)−Acc⁡(C1slot).\mathrm{Rep}=\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C3b})-\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C1}_{\mathrm{slot}}). (4)

In plain language, the repetition gap measures how much accuracy changes when one candidate is repeated instead of shown once in the multi-slot interface. Negative Rep means Duplicate underperforms Single-slot; positive Rep means Duplicate outperforms Single-slot. The baseline dependence of the two diversity contrasts is explicit in the identity

DSVslot−DSVdup=Rep,\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}-\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=\mathrm{Rep}, (5)

equivalently DSVdup=DSVslot−Rep\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}-\mathrm{Rep}.

3.5 Candidate-context values

After the comparisons above, we define candidate-context contrasts versus Direct:

CCVslot\displaystyle\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{slot}} =Acc⁡(C1slot)−Acc⁡(C2),\displaystyle=\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C1}_{\mathrm{slot}})-\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C2}), (6)
CCVdup\displaystyle\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{dup}} =Acc⁡(C3b)−Acc⁡(C2).\displaystyle=\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C3b})-\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C2}). (7)

Accounting identities then split the same CIV under either baseline:

CIV=DSVdup+CCVdup=DSVslot+CCVslot.\mathrm{CIV}=\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}+\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}+\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{slot}}. (8)

CIV itself does not depend on choosing Duplicate versus Single-slot; what changes is the DSV/CCV split. We call these terms candidate-context value because they mix candidate quality, text presence, repetition or interface structure, and aggregator reaction. They are accounting contrasts, not pure causal mediators.

3.6 What the measures do not identify

Repetition changes the input interface and can influence aggregator behavior. Single-slot changes candidate amount and coverage relative to Multi-candidate. Separately generated candidates can differ in quality, correctness, and content. Neither DSV contrast alone identifies pure causal diversity.

4 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks and units.

FRAMES (Krishna et al., 2025) (sampling n=200n{=}200; evidence n=180n{=}180) and MultiHopRAG (Tang and Yang, 2024) (replication n=100n{=}100). FRAMES model diversity uses a pairwise analysis covering 3030 distinct items, not the generic FRAMES n=200n{=}200 pool. MultiHop model diversity averages three fixed k=2k{=}2 model-pair comparisons within each of n=100n{=}100 items.

Sources and aggregator.

Sampling (S), model (M), and evidence (E) diversify candidates. Sampling diversity uses three samples per generator, averaged across three generators. For evidence diversity on both benchmarks, candidates come from a fixed Qwen3.8-Flash generator, and the Direct reference is the matched evidence-conditioned Direct, rather than union-evidence or closed-book Direct. The main aggregator (“Luna”) sees parsed final answers. Many confirmatory runs use a 1024-token output limit; later checks and the matched stronger-candidate extension use 4096. A Qwen3-32B extension keeps candidate content fixed and swaps the aggregator configuration (model plus decoding and reasoning settings), not a model-only intervention with equal decoding. Verified model labels, decoding settings, and prompt locations appear in Appendix M. Table B (Appendix B) summarizes datasets, panel sizes, token ceilings, and analysis status.

Scoring and analysis status.

We use exact/normalized string match, then a frozen semantic judge (Zheng et al., 2023). Unless noted, we report paired complete-case estimates with bootstrap 95% CIs (B=2000B{=}2000, seed 2026 where specified); no pp-values. Historical primary analyses, later controlled extensions, and exploratory diagnostics are distinguished in Appendix C (Table C); model settings and prompt sources appear in Appendix M. The historical primary S/M/E analyses use DSV=DSVdup\mathrm{DSV}=\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}. We do not relabel all later results as confirmatory.

Human audit.

We audited a late-stage stratified sample of n=60n{=}60 judged responses (seed 2026; twelve cases from each of five strata), not a simple random sample of the completed judged universe. Two independent raters adjudicated eight disagreements. Versus final human labels, the judge agreed on 50/6050/60 (83.3%83.3\%; κ=0.645\kappa{=}0.645). False rejections on this packet are mostly paraphrase or alias mismatches on FRAMES aggregator answers. The audit does not support a CIV/DSV/CCV correction (Appendix E; Tables E and E).

5 Control-Dependent Ensemble Value

Table 1 reports the historical Duplicate-relative decomposition (plotted in Appendix A), motivating the matched Single-slot and repetition-gap analyses that follow. Evidence CIV (Multi-candidate minus Direct) is strongly negative on both benchmarks, while evidence DSVdup\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}} is near zero: most of the loss is candidate-context value, not a baseline-specific diversity increment. This differs from settings where designed evidence asymmetry is intended to help deliberation (Li et al., 2026). On MultiHop models, DSVdup=+9.3\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=+9.3 pp while CIV is −3.0-3.0 pp: a positive gain over Duplicate does not imply a positive candidate gain over Direct. Sampling effects are smaller and task-dependent (near zero CIV on FRAMES; negative CIV on MultiHop). We therefore first test whether the Duplicate baseline itself can depress accuracy, then test whether the pattern changes under a matched stronger-candidate extension.

Control dependence.

Under the same MultiHop model panel (n=100n{=}100), gain over Single-slot is only DSVslot=+1.00\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}=+1.00 pp [−2.33,+4.67][-2.33,+4.67], while the repetition gap is Rep=−8.33\mathrm{Rep}=-8.33 pp [−13.25,−3.75][-13.25,-3.75], so DSVdup=DSVslot−Rep\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}-\mathrm{Rep} recovers +9.33+9.33 pp (Figure 2a). Under negative Rep, DSVdup\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}} exceeds DSVslot\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}} by −Rep-\mathrm{Rep}. This does not make DSVdup\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}} wrong; it measures a different contrast. A CI that includes zero means the contrast is unresolved at this precision, not that the effect is zero. The MultiHop model-diversity result is control-sensitive: DSVdup\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}} and DSVslot\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}} tell different stories. We next ask whether the same control dependence appears when the candidate-generation configuration is strengthened on FRAMES.

Stronger candidates under two controls.

Is a small Duplicate-relative DSV only a symptom of weak candidates? A weak panel can make both total CIV and diversity-related increments look small for uninteresting reasons. We therefore ask whether raising candidate quality changes the picture when the aggregator and item set stay matched. We compare an original candidate panel with a higher-performing panel generated using different models and generation settings. We hold the questions, panel size (k=3k{=}3), aggregator (Luna), and aggregator output limit (4096 tokens) fixed, on n=200n{=}200 FRAMES items (the original 9595-item cohort plus a completed nonoverlapping 105105-item complement). The original panel uses Solar Mini4, Qwen3.8-Flash, and Haiku 4.5 with temperature 0.00.0 and a 10241024-token candidate-output limit (no explicit reasoning effort set). The stronger panel uses Gemini 3.8 Flash, Grok 4.7, and Sonnet 5.5 with temperature 0.00.0, reasoning effort high, and a 6553665536-token candidate-output limit. The 4096-token aggregation limit is distinct from these candidate-generation limits. The resulting contrast measures the value of replacing the candidate-generation configuration, not the isolated effect of model identity under equal candidate-generation compute.

Contrasts are stronger minus original (paired bootstrap, B=2000B{=}2000, seed 2026). Improving the candidate-generation configuration raises CIV by +20.50+20.50 pp [+14.00,+27.00][+14.00,+27.00]. Table 2 reports the absolute arm accuracies, which clarify the within-panel signs. Table 3 reports the matched changes. On the matched FRAMES items, the original Multi-candidate panel is below Direct (41.5%41.5\% versus 46.5%46.5\%; CIV ≈−5.0\approx-5.0 pp), whereas the stronger panel is above Direct (62.0%62.0\% versus 46.5%46.5\%; CIV ≈+15.5\approx+15.5 pp). This reversal corresponds to the paired Δ​CIV=+20.50\Delta\mathrm{CIV}=+20.50 pp, while the attributed additional-candidate contrast changes by +0.67+0.67 pp under Duplicate versus +10.33+10.33 pp under Single-slot. The key paired contrast is Δ​Rep=+9.67\Delta\mathrm{Rep}=+9.67 pp [+6.00,+13.50][+6.00,+13.50]: it directly shows that the two diversity attributions differ, rather than relying on one Δ\DeltaDSV CI excluding zero and another including zero (Figure 2b; Figure 3). On the original panel, Rep=−6.33\mathrm{Rep}=-6.33 pp [−9.33,−3.67][-9.33,-3.67] (Duplicate worse than Single-slot). On the stronger panel, Rep=+3.33\mathrm{Rep}=+3.33 pp [+0.83,+5.83][+0.83,+5.83] (Duplicate better than Single-slot). Thus Δ​DSVslot=+10.33\Delta\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}}=+10.33 pp and Δ​DSVdup=+0.67\Delta\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=+0.67 pp are different splits of the same Δ\DeltaCIV, linked by Δ​Rep\Delta\mathrm{Rep}. Context shifts are Δ​CCVdup=+19.83\Delta\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=+19.83 pp [+15.17,+24.67][+15.17,+24.67] and Δ​CCVslot=+10.17\Delta\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{slot}}=+10.17 pp [+6.33,+14.17][+6.33,+14.17].

Answer-count sensitivity.

A separate controlled intervention on eligible mixed-answer cases finds that changing answer multiplicity changes aggregation accuracy by +8.12+8.12 pp [+4.99,+11.42][+4.99,+11.42] (n=197n{=}197). This supports sensitivity to answer counts but does not establish the mechanism behind the repetition-gap differences observed across candidate-generation configurations.

The n=95n{=}95/n=105n{=}105 rows are same-protocol diagnostics, not independent benchmarks (Appendix D, Table D). The MultiHop model-diversity contrast used pairwise k=2k{=}2; the matched FRAMES extension uses k=3k{=}3, so they are not independent replications of one intervention. Earlier standalone-candidate evaluations used a different stack and are reported separately in Appendix H; their estimates are not pooled with the matched comparison. An exploratory candidate-conditioned breakdown suggests that repetition effects vary with candidate correctness; all four correctness-by-panel cells are reported in Appendix L. Correctness is post-generation and is not a causal mediator. Slot-prompt position and placeholder variants on an n=60n{=}60 subset keep positive Δ​DSVslot\Delta\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}} point estimates while variant-minus-primary CIs include zero (Appendix K). The Single-slot contrast measures incremental value over a single-filled-slot control, not pure causal diversity.

6 Information Loss Beyond Baseline Choice

Lost information through candidates.

Making information available is not the same as extracting it into candidate answers, and extracting it is not the same as the aggregator using it (Liu et al., 2024). On FRAMES, candidates-only accuracy (47.2%47.2\%) is far below RAW (65.6%65.6\%), and RAW+candidates (65.7%65.7\%) returns almost to RAW. On MultiHop, recovery is only +6.0+6.0 pp (91.091.0 / 74.774.7 / 80.780.7), so candidate context can still hurt (Figure 4a). We do not claim a position-bias mechanism.

Output-limit check.

Re-running FRAMES evidence aggregation at 4096 tokens (n=180n{=}180) lowers Multi-candidate evidence truncation from 20.4%20.4\% to 1.7%1.7\%, but CIVE moves from −15.9-15.9 pp to −18.33-18.33 pp [−24.26,−12.03][-24.26,-12.03]. CCVslot≈−17.56\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{slot}}\approx-17.56 pp and CCVdup≈−18.70\mathrm{CCV}_{\mathrm{dup}}\approx-18.70 pp remain strongly negative under both baselines (Figure 4b). CIV itself is unchanged by the choice of non-diverse baseline; the empirical finding is that both candidate-context contrasts stay strongly negative. Short outputs do not explain the evidence gap. On robustness subsets, a second aggregator family shows the same qualitative pattern: evidence CIV stays strongly negative with near-zero evidence DSV, while model DSV can be positive (Appendix G, Table G).

Control robustness.

The remaining evidence checks distinguish information preserved in raw evidence, extracted into candidates, and used by the aggregator. The corresponding evidence repetition gap is small at the observed point estimate, Rep≈−1.15\mathrm{Rep}\approx-1.15 pp [−4.23,+2.01][-4.23,+2.01] (Appendix J). This interval does not establish that Duplicate and Single-slot are equivalent.

Additional checks.

Visible full explanations do not clearly raise DSVdup\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}} in our checks (FRAMES −0.67-0.67; MultiHop −2.33-2.33; both CIs include zero); a compact-rationale follow-up is similarly unresolved (Appendix I, Table I). Trace-level synthesis is methodologically different from our answer-level checks (Fadnavis et al., 2026). These secondary checks are reported in the appendix and do not change the evidence-loss result.

7 Discussion and Conclusion

The results imply several practices for ensemble evaluation and design.

Always report the baseline.

A diversity-related gain should state whether it is measured over Single-slot or Duplicate. On MultiHop model diversity (k=2k{=}2) and the matched FRAMES stronger-panel extension (k=3k{=}3), DSVdup\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}} and DSVslot\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{slot}} tell different design stories. If gain over Duplicate is large while gain over Single-slot is not, adding more models is not automatically justified by the Duplicate-relative number alone.

Do not assume repetition is neutral.

Matched FRAMES results show that Rep can change sign between candidate-generation configurations. This does not establish a universal causal mechanism for the sign change.

Candidate quality and diversity attribution are separate questions.

Improving the candidate-generation configuration can raise CIV without producing the same increase under every diversity-related contrast.

Restoring raw evidence recovers most of the FRAMES gap.

Evidence can be lost through candidate answers or aggregation; on FRAMES, restoring RAW beside candidates recovers most of the observed gap. MultiHop recovery is only partial.

Aggregator configuration is a distinct design variable.

Holding candidate content fixed, the Luna-versus-Qwen3-32B evidence CIV gap is +12.59+12.59 pp [+4.07,+21.11][+4.07,+21.11] on FRAMES and +11.0+11.0 pp [+4.67,+17.67][+4.67,+17.67] on MultiHop. These observed configuration differences show that generating candidates and realizing their information with an aggregator are distinct design questions. They are not equal-decoding/equal-reasoning model-only interventions, do not establish Qwen Rep, and do not imply a universal ordering.

Cost–accuracy implications.

Figure 6 (Appendix F) compares the plotted deployment cost and accuracy of the observed policies. In its evidence-backed panel, Direct has higher plotted accuracy at lower plotted cost than the displayed M, E, and M+E candidate-based policies, illustrating why a diversity-related DSV contrast alone does not establish that extra candidate-generation and aggregation calls are worthwhile compared with Direct. These are descriptive within-panel comparisons: policies use different token limits, and C2PRO also changes model setup, so Figure 6 does not establish a general cost-optimal or equal-reasoning-budget policy.

Conclusion.

For LLM ensembles, evaluation should state which counterfactual defines the measured gain, how much candidate information survives the interface, and which effects persist across controls. Reporting CIV, baseline-specific DSV/CCV, and Rep makes those distinctions visible.

8 Limitations

We use selected short-answer benchmarks and mainly answer-level aggregation. Visible-explanation checks do not cover hidden traces. Single-slot (C1slot) changes coverage as well as distinctness; Duplicate (C3b) changes repetition; neither is a pure causal diversity estimand. The matched stronger-versus-original contrast changes candidate models and generation settings together, so it is not a model-only effect at equal candidate-generation compute. Evidence-diversity findings use a single fixed candidate generator on both benchmarks, so their transfer to other generators is untested.

Headline tests primarily use one aggregator (Luna); Qwen CIV gaps do not establish Qwen Rep. The human audit is a stratified n=60n{=}60 packet and does not demonstrate absence of arm-differential judge error on the matched Single-slot/Duplicate cells; we do not numerically correct main effects. Aggregation truncation was tracked, and the frozen inclusion policy was retained rather than switching to success-only accuracy. We do not claim a complete candidate-generation empty/parse-failure comparison between panels beyond the disclosed generation-config differences and aggregation-arm health checks.

Candidate-conditioned Rep analyses are exploratory and condition on a post-generation variable. Slot position/placeholder variants (n=60n{=}60) do not prove equivalence of prompt forms. Later extensions were motivated by earlier findings; they are not all confirmatory. Public OpenRouter slugs and decoding settings appear in Appendix M; vendor-internal build IDs remain unresolved.

Appendix E Human Audit Details

Late-stage stratified sample: twelve cases from each of five judged strata (standard S/M/E, factorial evidence-layout manipulation, MultiHop replication, Kimi robustness, and alternate Direct configuration C2-Pro; seed 2026), drawn from the then-available judged universe and not redrawn after later call completion. Two raters labeled Correct / Incorrect / Ambiguous, blinded to judge decisions; eight disagreements were adjudicated.

All ten FN cases on this packet are FRAMES aggregator paraphrase, alias, or unit-equivalent mismatches. One FRAMES audit case (A05) was flagged for external AI assistance during labeling; excluding it gives human–judge agreement 49/5949/59 (vs. 50/6050/60 overall), with specificity unchanged. We do not invent additional assistance flags or recalibrate experimental contrasts.

Appendix I Compact Rationale (Exploratory)

Answer-only (A0) places only the parsed answer in each candidate slot. Compact visible rationale (R1) appends a sentence-boundary-respecting prefix of the visible explanation, truncated to K=200K{=}200 tokens with o200k_base; Full visible explanation (R2) appends the complete visible explanation. This exploratory comparison reuses stored stronger-panel candidate responses and their visible explanations, without new candidate generation or model-based summarization. The original candidate panel fell below the frozen 95% visible-explanation coverage requirement (FRAMES 29%; MultiHopRAG 47%) and was excluded. Here DSV is Duplicate-relative, DSVdup=Acc⁡(C1)−meani​Acc​(C3bi)\mathrm{DSV}_{\mathrm{dup}}=\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C1})-\mathrm{mean}_{i}\,\mathrm{Acc}(\mathrm{C3b}_{i}), so the rows are changes in that contrast between representations; KK is rationale-prefix length, not panel size kk.
